preface.para: Fire is a FHIR R5 server generated from HL7's definitions. This is its Scaly form: a program written in Scaly that serves the same API on the same database as the C# server the generator was first written for.

partintro.para: This part describes the design of Fire and the procedures of its development.

chapter.title: Design
chapter.para: The following sections describe the components of Fire and its design principles.

sect1.title: Components
sect1.para: Fire consists of a model, a generator, a runtime and the program the generator writes.

sect2.title: FHIR Server
sect2.para: The FHIR server stores data as FHIR resources and allows you to

listitem.para: read, write and query them with FHIR searches through the FHIR RESTful API,
send batch and transaction bundles,
and
browse and edit resources through the built-in HTML pages.

sect2.para: The server is one executable. It is made of two parts:

listitem.para: The Scaly package packages/fhir, written by hand. It knows nothing of a particular resource: handlers, repository, search, validation, bundles and the output formats all work from the model they are handed.
server/fire.scaly, written by the generator. It holds the model as one text of records and hands it to the runtime.

sect2.title: Code Generator
sect2.para: The generator is written in DSSSL. From the XML model it writes the program, the model's records, the SQL of the database schema for the three databases, the JavaScript of the HTML pages and the reference pages of this documentation.

sect2.title: The C# Server
sect2.para: The directory upstream holds the generator this one descends from. It writes a C# server from the same model. The Scaly server is measured against it: it answers with the same bytes and keeps the same tables with the same contents, so either server can continue on a database the other one wrote.
Where the C# server does something it should not, the Scaly server does the same as long as the answers or the stored rows would differ otherwise. Limitations lists what a user can see of that.

sect1.title: Design Principles
sect1.para: The following sections describe the data layout, the repository layer, the storage of the content and how a request is served.

sect2.title: Data Model
sect2.para: For each resource type there is a resource table with the resource's name (e.g. Patient) and a schema of the same name which holds its history and search tables. SQLite has no schemas; there the schema's name is the front part of the table's name (Patient_search_name).

listitem.para: The resource table, one row per resource: its id, its current version, the time of the last change, the content, and a column for each search parameter that is a single top-level property.
The earlier versions of a resource and the marks of its deletions. Present only for a resource with history.
The values of the search parameter [name], one row per value.
On PostgreSQL, the bytes of a Binary, kept apart from its content.

sect2.para: The table dbinfo holds the version of the schema.

sect2.title: Repository Layer
sect2.para: The repository layer

listitem.para: stores and loads resources,
searches for them by their search parameters,
and
maintains the schema.

sect2.para: It supports

listitem.para: PostgreSQL,
SQL Server,
and
SQLite.

sect2.para: There is one repository for all three. Its SQL is written as PostgreSQL reads it and rendered for the database in use when a statement is sent: the names of tables, the placeholders of parameters, the paging clause. What differs in meaning, such as the form of a time or the lock on a row, is decided where it occurs.
Every write is one transaction: the resource's row, the copy of the replaced version in the history, and the rows of the search tables. A transaction bundle is one transaction as a whole.
A search is answered with two statements: one counts the matches, one fetches the page. Nothing is kept between two pages of a search.

sect2.title: Content Storage
sect2.para: The content of a resource is stored as raw UTF-8 JSON bytes (BYTEA in PostgreSQL, VARBINARY in SQL Server, BLOB in SQLite), in the text the C# server's serializer writes. A read in JSON answers these bytes as they are. They are parsed only where a part of them is needed: for XML and HTML, inside a bundle, for the search tables, for a patch.

sect2.title: Serving a Request
sect2.para: The server runs a scheduler thread per processor core. A request is a task on one of them; where it waits for the database or the network, the thread serves other requests. Each thread has its own connections to the database.
The memory a request needs is taken from a region that is given back as a whole when the request is answered. There is no garbage collector.
The model is read once at the start and indexed; a handler looks up what it needs to know of a resource type by the type's name.

chapter.title: Development
chapter.para: This chapter describes the generation, how to build and test, and how this documentation is produced.

sect1.title: Generating Code
sect1.para: What the server knows of FHIR comes from an XML model, which is made of the FHIR specification.

listitem.para: The converter turns the JSON definitions of the specification into model/fhir.xml.
The model is edited: the resources to be served are activated.
The generator writes the program and the web root from the model.

sect2.title: The Converter
sect2.para: tools/fhir-to-xml is a Scaly program. It reads these files of the definitions:

listitem.para: The resources.
The data types.
The value sets and code systems.
The search parameters.

sect2.para: The model is kept in the repository, so a build needs neither the definitions nor the converter. tools/pin-model.sh makes it anew; tools/pin-model.sh --check says whether the converter still writes the kept model byte for byte.

sect2.title: Editing the XML Model
sect2.para: model/fhir.xml contains all resources and search parameters of the specification; model/fire.dtd is its DTD. A resource is served when its active attribute is true. The elements, with the plural elements and the id and name attributes left out:

listitem.para: A resource. active says whether the server serves it, history whether its versions are kept.
A data type, global or of a resource.
A property of a resource or an element. iscollection is true if it can occur more than once, notnull if it must occur.
A possible type of a property. ref links to the element or, for a code with a required binding, to the codeset.
A resource type a reference may point to.
A set of codes and a code of it.
A search parameter with its type.
A path of a search parameter, its steps through the properties, and the type a step is narrowed to.
A component of a composite search parameter.
A step that lifts a database of an earlier version of the model; see Database Schemas.

sect2.title: The Code Generator
sect2.para: The generator is run by dazzle, a DSSSL processor. DSSSL is the Document Style Semantics and Specification Language; the generator uses the SGML transformation back end, which writes files of text.
tools/generate.sh runs it. Nothing it writes is kept in the repository:

listitem.para: The program.

The model as records: the types with their members, the code sets, the search tables and how a resource's values reach them, the references, the sort keys, the CapabilityStatement. Written by codegen/model.scm and codegen/search.scm.
The SQL that creates the schema and its indexes, and the SQL of the upgrade steps, for each of the three databases.
The web root: the scripts of the HTML pages, a reference page for each resource, the pages of this documentation.

sect2.para: The stylesheet is codegen/scaly.dsl. The parts that do not depend on the language of the server (the names, the schema, the scripts, the pages) are the files of upstream/codegen, included and not copied.

sect1.para: Building needs the Scaly toolchain and dazzle.

sect2.title: Testing
sect2.para: The tests put the Scaly server beside the C# server. They start their own database: a container for PostgreSQL and SQL Server, a file for SQLite. FIRE_DATABASE chooses it (postgresql, sqlite, sqlserver).

listitem.para: Runs the test suite pyrtest, black-box tests over HTTP, against the server.

The two servers take turns on one database. Every answer (status, content type, body) and every row they write must be the same. The requests are the lines of tools/turns/queries.txt and tools/turns/steps.txt; a new piece of behaviour gets its lines there.
The same comparison for a changed model: resources without history, and a database lifted by upgrade steps.
Both servers under load.

sect1.title: Producing Documentation
sect1.para: This documentation is served by the server itself, at index.html.

sect2.title: Writing
sect2.para: The prose is written in DocBook, in the one file documentation/fire.xml. The reference pages of the resources are generated from the model.

sect2.title: Generating Documentation
sect2.para: tools/generate.sh writes the pages along with everything else: it runs dazzle with upstream/codegen/documentation.dsl on documentation/fire.xml.

partintro.para: This part is about planning an installation, deploying it, and maintaining it.

chapter.title: Planning
chapter.para: An installation needs a decision about the platform, the database, and what stands in front of the server.

sect1.title: Platform
sect1.para: The server is a native executable, built for the machine it runs on. It needs no runtime installed beside it. It has been built and tested on macOS on ARM; Scaly also builds for Linux and for Intel processors. It has not been run on Windows.
The libraries it loads are OpenSSL (for a connection to the database inside TLS) and SQLite.

sect1.title: Database
sect1.para: Fire stores its resources in PostgreSQL, SQL Server or SQLite. The tests pass on all three.

sect2.title: PostgreSQL
sect2.para: The first choice, and the one with the most experience behind it. The database named in the connection string must exist; the server creates everything inside it.

sect2.title: MS SQL Server
sect2.para: The server logs in with a user and a password; Windows authentication is not supported. It creates the database if it is not there. The session is encrypted unless the connection string says Encrypt=False, but the server's certificate is not verified.

sect2.title: SQLite
sect2.para: A file, and no database server: for development, tests and small installations. Only one write happens at a time. Searching without regard to case knows the letters of ASCII only for what is stored: a stored upper-case umlaut is not found.

sect1.title: In Front of the Server
sect1.para: The server listens on the loopback address, speaks HTTP without TLS and does not authenticate anyone, the administrative routes included. It is meant to stand behind a proxy that terminates TLS and decides who may ask.
A request's body may be 16 MB at most.

chapter.title: Deployment
chapter.para: An installation is the executable, the directory wwwroot, and, if wanted, a directory of seed data. It is configured by its environment.

sect1.title: Running
sect1.para: Start the executable in the directory that holds wwwroot, or name the web root with ASPNETCORE_WEBROOT. At its start the server reaches the database, creates or lifts the schema, and then listens. It ends with a status other than 0 when the database type is unknown (2), the database cannot be reached or prepared (3), or the port cannot be listened on (4).
/healthz says that the process is up, /readyz that the database answers.
The server does not handle signals: it ends at once when it is stopped, without waiting for the requests in flight.

sect1.title: In Place of the C# Server
sect1.para: The settings have the names the C# server reads them by, so the same environment starts either. The database needs no conversion in either direction. The C# server reads appsettings.json as well; the Scaly server reads the environment alone.

sect1.title: Configuring
sect1.para: The settings are variables of the environment:

listitem.para: PostgreSql (the default), SqlServer or Sqlite.

In the form the .NET drivers read, the keywords without regard to case. PostgreSQL: Host=localhost;Port=5432;Database=Fire;Username=postgres;Password=…. SQL Server: Server=localhost,1433;Database=Fire;User Id=sa;Password=…;TrustServerCertificate=True. SQLite: Data Source=fire.db.
The address to listen on; its port is used. The default is 5080.
The directory of the web root. The default is wwwroot where the server is started. Without that directory the server serves no files.
The directory of the seed data. The default is seed where the server is started.
The secret of the reseed route. Without it that route refuses.
PostgreSQL: the number of connections the server may hold.

chapter.title: Maintenance
chapter.para: This chapter describes the management of the database schema and browsing, editing and deleting data with the server itself.

sect1.title: Database Schemas
sect1.para: On an empty database the server creates all schemas, tables and indexes at its start, and loads the seed data.

On a database of an earlier version of the model it carries out the model's upgrade steps, each in a transaction of its own: the step's SQL, the search tables it adds filled from the stored resources, and then the new version. A step that needs a program of its own (a data migration) is not supported; the server names it and does not start.
The routes of this section are not protected by the server; see In Front of the Server.

sect1.title: Browsing and Deleting Data
sect1.para: A browser that asks the server gets HTML. Enter a FHIR search URL to get a bundle page, or the address of a resource to get its resource page.

sect2.title: Bundle Page
sect2.para: A search such as
is shown as a table. The page lets you

listitem.para: delete selected resources, or all that match the search,
download the result as a JSON bundle,
go through the pages of the result,
and
go to a resource by its link.

sect2.title: Resource Page
sect2.para: The resource page lets you

listitem.para: inspect and edit a resource,
go to the resources it refers to,
and
find the resources that refer to it.

sect2.para: Download JSON saves the resource as a file, History shows its versions.

Below the editing area there is a line for each resource type that can refer to the current resource, with a link for each of its reference search parameters. A link searches for the resources of that type which refer to the current one.

sect1.title: Editing Resources
sect1.para: To change a resource:

listitem.para: To add an element, click the + button beside the field's name and enter the data.
To remove an element, click the - button.
To edit a reference, select edit in the list before the link. link shows it as a link again, - removes it.
Click Save.

sect1.para: To create a resource, click New, enter its data and click Save.
To take back the current version of a resource, click Rollback and confirm.

chapter.title: FHIR Functionality
chapter.para: The server implements FHIR R5 for the resources that are active in the model; the resource list names them. /fire/metadata answers the CapabilityStatement.

sect1.title: FHIR API
sect1.para: The base address is /fire.

sect2.title: REST

listitem.para: Read. A deleted resource answers 410, an unknown id 404. If-None-Match answers 304 for what the client has.
Read of a version.
Create. With If-None-Exist only when the search it holds finds nothing.
Update, or create under the given id. With If-Match only when the version is the one named.
Conditional update.
A change by JSON Patch.
Delete, and conditional delete.
The history of a resource, of a type and of everything.
Search.
A Bundle of type batch or transaction.

sect2.para: A write answers with the resource; the Prefer header (return=minimal, return=OperationOutcome) changes that. A resource is validated before it is stored: its members and their types, the codes of a required binding, the members that must be there. An X-Provenance header stores a Provenance for the write.
A read of a Binary answers its bytes under their own content type unless the request asks for FHIR.

sect2.title: Formats
sect2.para: The server reads JSON. It answers in JSON, in XML, or as an HTML page that shows the resource. The parameter _format decides (json, xml, html, or a media type); without it the Accept header does: application/fhir+json or application/json, then application/fhir+xml, then anything with html in it. Everything else is answered in JSON.

sect2.title: Operations
sect2.para: The operations beyond the standard are autocomplete, undelete, rollback and import. The operations FHIR defines for a resource ($validate, $everything and the like) are not implemented.

listitem.para: A resource can be sent in JSON only.

The XML form is not the XML of the FHIR specification: a resource inside a Bundle loses the element that names its type, and the url of an extension and the id of an element are written as child elements. Use JSON to exchange data.
In the HTML form, a --> inside the data is shown as -/->.
The _since parameter of a history is not looked at.
The addresses in the history of everything (/fire/_history) begin with /fhir.
There are no subscriptions, no terminology services and no authentication.

sect1.title: Querying
sect1.para: A search is a GET on the resource type with its conditions in the query, or a POST to _search with them in a form.

sect2.title: Introduction
sect2.para: Supported are

listitem.para: the modifiers :exact, :contains, :missing and :not, and the prefixes of numbers and dates (eq, ne, gt, lt, ge, le, sa, eb, ap);
several values in one condition (or) and a condition given several times (and);
chained parameters (subject.name=…) and reverse chains (_has);
_include and _revinclude, also with :iterate;
composite parameters;
_sort, _count and _offset for paging, _total, _summary and _elements.

sect2.para: /fire/SearchParameter?base={Resource} lists the search parameters of a resource.

listitem.para: A search parameter the server does not know is refused with 400, not passed over. That includes _text, _content and _filter, which are not implemented.
_format in the query of a search is refused the same way. Ask for XML or HTML of a search with the Accept header.
The search parameter phonetic does no phonetic matching. It is answered exactly like name: a search for phonetic=Meier finds what name=Meier finds, and does not find Mayer or Maier.
_sort by a whole name is refused; sort by family or given.

sect1.title: Extended API
sect1.para: What the server offers beyond FHIR.

sect2.title: Autocomplete
sect2.para: Each resource type has a GET /fire/{Resource}/$autocomplete operation that answers the matching values of a search table as a plain JSON array of strings. The query is that of a search: a working search URL becomes an autocomplete by putting $autocomplete into its path.
Names of patients that begin with "smi": /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?name=smi
The family names of the patients whose name matches "smi": /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?name=smi&_autocomplete=family
The name of a resource by its id, which the HTML pages use to show a reference: /fire/Patient/$autocomplete?_id=123&_autocomplete=name
The answer:

listitem.para: A search parameter and the beginning of its value, without regard to case; for _id the whole id. The parameter can be _id, a string parameter, or a token parameter with a table of its own (e.g. identifier), not one that is a column of the resource table.
The search parameter whose values are answered, when it is another one than the one searched.
How many values to answer at most, and how many to skip.

sect2.title: Importing
sect2.para: PUT /fire/{Resource}/_history/{id} stores a resource under the given id without the checks of an update: it is not validated and no version is asked for. It is meant for moving data in from another system.
